_source: Ryan Boren's brief, 2026-11-03: a restaurant on the street to hang out in when he eats, with a broader palette of dishes than Vital Plant Living, after the Mediterranean and Okinawan ways of cooking he eats from, with fusion dishes of the two; first and foremost for him and his tastes, and a prescription for nobody. Ryan chose the name the same day, from Claude's suggestions. Read by tools/make-champuru.py.
_menu: Every dish is Hey, Good Cookin's shape (name, diet, what, animal, note) and goes through that room's check_dish, so its allergen line is worked out from `what` and can never disagree with it; every drink's caffeine is worked out by Pekoe and Purrs'. A sauce or a spice mix is spelled out (tahini, not hummus alone; sesame seeds, not za'atar alone) so the engine can read it. Each note says where the dish comes from and what it is, and never what it does for anybody.

name.culture: the word is sometimes used for the culture of Okinawa itself, a mixture of traditional Okinawan, Chinese, mainland Japanese, Southeast Asian and North American culture

_ryan: Ryan's own words, from his brief of 2026-11-03, exactly as he wrote them. They are quoted as his and are not swept for the room's refusals, because they are his to say.
ryan: I want to create a restaurant on Stimpunks.World to hang out in when I eat. I use Vital Plant Living often, but I want another spot with a broader palette of dishes that reflects the rest of my diet.
This restaurant is first and foremost for me and my personal tastes and not a prescription for anyone else.

_kitchen: Said on the page so the menu cannot pass for how Okinawa eats: Okinawan home cooking uses a good deal of pork and SPAM (Wikipedia's chanpurū article says so of the champuru), and this kitchen cooks those dishes with tofu, egg and fish because it is Ryan's.
kitchen: Okinawan home cooking uses a good deal of pork, and SPAM, which came with the American military, and a champuru there is as likely to have either in it as tofu. This kitchen cooks its Okinawan dishes with tofu, egg and fish, and its Greek and Moroccan ones without the lamb, because it is Ryan’s kitchen and that is how he eats. Nothing on this menu says how anybody else eats, in Okinawa or round the Mediterranean or anywhere.
rules: Every dish says what is in it before you order it, and its allergens are worked out from those words.
Nothing on the menu says what a dish does for a body. It is food, and it is what Ryan likes.
Nobody counts anything here: not what is on your plate, not how often you come.
The menu changes when Ryan asks, and only then.
You are welcome at this table whatever you eat. The table is Ryan’s and the menu is his, and neither is advice for you.
